catalog_quote: [Odden 2006: 59] Penult-H data like [ni mu'ka60] shows that the restriction against H-shifting from the copula is not simply due to the fact of there being a following H: rather, it is a final H that blocks tone shift. Descriptively, we can say that a H is blocked from associating to a vowel before a final H, or that it is blocked from associating to a stressed vowel before a H, insofar as penult stress is automatic in the language. [Odden 2006: 35 fn.1] Unlike Dembwa, which allows both level H and falling tone on the penult, in Mbololo, the phrasal penult is somewhat lengthened, but the length of the penult has no phonological consequences, a H toned penult always having level H pitch. new_statements.rule_in_words: Dawida is a (restricted) tone language with lexical H vs. toneless syllables and rightward H shift; independently of tone, prominence (stress) falls automatically on the penultimate syllable, realized chiefly as predictable lengthening of the penult of the phrase/pre-pausal word (Odden 2001: 75, 80 for Dembwa; Odden 2006: 35 for Mbololo). Corroborated by Sakamoto 2003: 13 ('the stress of a word almost always falls on the last syllable but one', e.g. mómu, iríso, irídia, irughúdia) and Philippson 1991: 512 (penult bears an 'accent demarcatif (culmination de longueur)').
new_statements.exceptions: Sakamoto 2003 says 'almost always' without listing exceptions; Sakamoto 2008 notes one future tense 'slightly throwing the accent on the final syllable of the verb' (Nilimá 'I will cultivate'). Odden gives none.
new_statements.domain_note: Odden's lengthening is explicitly the penult of the phrase (pre-pausal): ku-bóona 'to see' but ku-bona baandu 'to see people' (2001: 80); 'penult stress is automatic' is stated without a domain but his examples are phrase-final citation forms. Sakamoto frames it as word stress on citation forms. Stress is non-contrastive; tone is the lexical prosodic contrast.
new_statements.identity_note: All statements concern Dawida proper (E74a = Glottolog tait1250, iso dav): Odden 2006 describes the Mbololo dialect, Odden 2001 the Dembwa dialect, Philippson 1991/2014 the Josa (and Werugha) dialects, Sakamoto 'Kidawida' of the Taita Hills generally. Saghala/Sagalla (E74b, saga1262, iso tga; Wray 1894) is a separate language and was excluded. Kasigau (E74c) is treated as a Dawida dialect by Sakamoto; none of the quoted statements is specific to it.
